The core insight is that soccer is a spatial game where possession and disruption are governed by continuous fields over the pitch. The authors define a Gaussian process-based model to estimate possession control and defensive disruption as functions of spatial coordinates. The model uses regression coefficients αatk and βdef to weight offensive and defensive contributions, and a spatial GP Z(s) to encode local variations in these behaviors. This dual-field representation allows for a unified framework to analyze both offensive control and defensive pressure. The disruption surface D(s) is derived from pass interruption events, while the control surface C(s) reflects possession retention. These surfaces are then aggregated into team-specific maps that reveal tactical profiles. The model’s strength lies in its ability to translate discrete event data into continuous spatial representations, enabling comparative analysis of team strategies and managerial influence. Failure modes include misalignment of spatial resolution with actual tactical granularity or overfitting due to limited sample size.
